title: The history of atomic models
summary: How were atomic models built to explain experimental results, and how did they develop?
olay.h: The gold foil that changed the model of the atom
olay.p: Geiger and Marsden fired alpha particles at a very thin gold foil. What they saw could not be explained by the atomic model of the day. In this lesson you will do the same experiment.
cards.0.p: An atom is too small to see, even with a microscope. Scientists built models that explain experimental results. When a new experiment could not be explained, the model changed.
cards.0.etk.soru: Put the atomic models in the order they appeared, from oldest to newest.
cards.0.once.soru: You cannot see inside a closed box. How can you find out what is in it?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: When you cannot see, you experiment and build a model from the results. This is how scientists studied the atom.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: Even if you cannot see inside, experiments can tell you what is there.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: A guess with no experiment behind it cannot be tested. A model must rest on experimental results.
cards.1.p: Democritus (5th century BCE) said that if you keep dividing matter, you finally reach particles that cannot be divided. He called them atomos. This was a philosophical idea, not an experiment, and it was not accepted for centuries.
cards.1.once.soru: You cut a piece of gold in half, then in half again. Can you keep doing this forever?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: In the end you reach the smallest piece of gold, a gold atom. Democritus thought the same and called this particle atomos.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: Matter cannot be divided forever. In the end you reach an atom.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: The gold does not vanish. The smallest piece of gold is a gold atom.
cards.2.p: Dalton (1803) pictured atoms as solid spheres that cannot be divided. In his view, atoms of the same element are identical and combine in compounds in a fixed ratio. Once electrons and isotopes were found, this model was no longer enough.
cards.2.svg#4: Explained: conservation of mass, fixed ratios
cards.2.once.soru: Water always forms in a ratio of 1 gram of hydrogen to 8 grams of oxygen. How did Dalton explain this?
cards.2.once.secenekler.0.neden: Every water molecule has the same number of H and O atoms. That is why the mass ratio is always the same.
cards.2.once.secenekler.1.neden: The ratio comes out the same every time. If it were random, it would vary.
cards.2.once.secenekler.2.neden: In Dalton's view, atoms do not turn into other atoms.
cards.2.key: Atoms of the same element with different masses are called isotopes. You will see isotopes in the topic on the structure of the atom.
cards.3.p: In 1897 Thomson showed that cathode (negative terminal) rays are made of negatively charged electrons. In his model the atom was a positively charged sphere with electrons embedded in it like raisins.
cards.4.h: Millikan: the charge of the electron
cards.4.p: In 1909 Millikan held charged oil droplets suspended between two plates. The charges he measured always came out as whole multiples of 1.6·10⁻¹⁹ C. This value is the charge of one electron.
cards.4.key: Charge is quantized. Every charge is a whole multiple of the electron's charge.
cards.4.once.soru: The charge of oil drops is measured. The results always come out as 1, 2, 3... times 1.6·10⁻¹⁹ C. What does this show?
cards.4.once.secenekler.0.neden: The smallest piece of charge is the charge of one electron, and every charge is a whole multiple of it.
cards.4.once.secenekler.1.neden: Measurement errors would scatter the results at random. Getting whole multiples every time is a rule.
cards.4.once.secenekler.2.neden: No values in between ever showed up, because charge is quantized.
cards.5.p: This result could not be explained by Thomson's model, because positive charge spread everywhere could not turn an alpha particle back. Rutherford described it like this: "You fire a shell at a sheet of tissue paper, and it comes back."
cards.6.p: For Rutherford (1911), since most particles passed through the foil, the atom must be mostly empty space. The positive charge and the mass are packed into a very small nucleus. The electrons move around this nucleus.
cards.6.key: This model had a problem. An orbiting electron should give off energy and fall into the nucleus.
cards.7.p: In 1919 Rutherford found the positive particle in the nucleus, the proton. But the mass of nuclei was more than the protons could account for. In 1932 Chadwick found the uncharged neutron.
cards.7.svg#0: Discovering the particles in an atom
cards.7.svg#16: Without neutrons, the mass would not add up.
cards.7.key: The particles of the atom were discovered in this order: electron (1897), proton (1919) and neutron (1932).
cards.7.once.soru: A helium nucleus has 2 protons, but its mass is close to 4 protons. Where does the extra mass come from?
cards.7.once.secenekler.0.neden: The nucleus also holds uncharged neutrons. Because they have no charge, they were found last, in 1932.
cards.7.once.secenekler.1.neden: An electron is about 1836 times lighter than a proton. So it cannot explain the difference.
cards.7.once.secenekler.2.neden: The difference showed up regularly in every nucleus. So it was something real.
cards.8.p: For Bohr (1913), electrons move only in certain energy levels and lose no energy there. When an electron drops to a lower level, it gives off light of a certain color. But this model worked only for particles with a single electron.
cards.8.key: An electron absorbs energy when it moves up a level and gives it off as light when it drops down.
cards.9.h: The modern model: the electron cloud
cards.9.p: In the modern model there is no exact orbit. Quantum mechanics only lets us calculate the probability of finding the electron in a region. These regions are called orbitals.
cards.10.p:
• Democritus put forward the idea of the indivisible atomos.
• Dalton pictured the atom as a solid sphere. Thomson found the electron, and Millikan measured its charge.
• Rutherford found the small, positive nucleus. The atom is mostly empty space.
• Bohr proposed energy levels. The modern model describes orbitals.
quiz.0.q: Match each experiment or observation with the model it showed to be incomplete.
quiz.0.ciftler.1.0: Particles bouncing back from gold foil
quiz.0.e: The electron showed that the atom can be divided, which left Dalton's model incomplete. Particles bouncing back revealed the small nucleus, which left Thomson's model incomplete. Rutherford could not explain the line spectrum. Bohr's model failed for many-electron atoms.
quiz.1.q: Match each experiment or finding with the scientist.
quiz.1.ciftler.0.0: Discovering the electron with cathode rays
quiz.1.e: Thomson found the electron with cathode rays, and Millikan measured its charge with oil drops. The gold foil experiment was done under Rutherford's direction, Chadwick found the neutron, and Bohr explained the hydrogen spectrum.
quiz.2.q: Sort each model by whether the atom has a nucleus.
quiz.2.e: Dalton thought of the atom as a solid sphere, and Thomson as electrons embedded in a positive sphere. Neither had the idea of a nucleus. Rutherford found the nucleus. Bohr's model and the modern model describe the electrons around the nucleus.
quiz.3.q: In the gold foil experiment, what does it show that a few alpha particles bounced back?
quiz.3.o.0: Most of the atom is empty space
quiz.3.o.1: Mass and positive charge are packed into a tiny nucleus
quiz.3.o.3: Positive charge is spread evenly through the atom
quiz.3.e: To bounce back, a particle must meet a very strong push. That only happens if the positive charge and mass are packed into a very small volume.
quiz.3.y.0: Most particles go straight through the empty space. Bouncing back points to a strong push.
quiz.3.y.2: Electrons are negatively charged and much lighter than an alpha particle. So they cannot turn it back.
quiz.3.y.3: Spread-out positive charge, as in Thomson's model, pushes only weakly. It cannot turn a fast alpha particle back.
A:ozet: Try it first, then learn its name. Deflect a cathode ray, fire particles at gold foil and drop an electron to a lower level.
A:adimlar.0.metin: In 1897 J. J. Thomson passed cathode rays between two charged plates in a tube with the air pumped out.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.soru: Which plate does the ray bend toward?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: The ray was pulled toward the positive plate, so it is made of negatively charged particles. These particles are called electrons. Since electrons come from atoms, the atom can be divided, and Dalton's solid sphere falls short.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Opposite charges attract and like charges repel. Which plate did the ray move toward?
A:adimlar.0.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: An uncharged ray would not bend. This ray is made of charged particles.
A:adimlar.1.metin: This sphere in Thomson's pudding model has 6 units of positive charge. Add electrons to make the atom neutral.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.tamam: 6 negative charges balance 6 positive charges, and the atom as a whole has no charge. For Thomson, the positive charge was spread throughout the sphere.
A:adimlar.2.metin: In 1909, under Rutherford's direction, Geiger and Marsden fired positively charged alpha particles at a very thin gold foil. By Thomson's model, nearly all of them should have gone straight through.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: What do you think the particles did?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: Most passed, a few bounced back
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Most particles going straight through shows that most of the atom is empty space. The drawing exaggerates the particles bouncing back. In reality only about 1 in 8000 bounced back.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: That is what Thomson's model predicted, but the experiment gave a different result.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The foil is very thin, and the atom is mostly empty space. So most particles hit nothing.
A:adimlar.3.metin: Bring the alpha particle closer to the nucleus and make it bounce back.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.tamam: Only a particle that gets very close to the nucleus is pushed back by its positive charge. The nucleus is about 100 000 times smaller than the atom, so this is very rare. Most particles pass through empty space.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.ipucu: Reduce the distance and play again.
A:adimlar.4.metin: For Bohr, hydrogen's electron can only be in certain levels. The electron is now in level 3. Drop it to level 2.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.tamam: As the electron dropped to the lower level, it gave off the energy difference as light of a certain color. A drop from level 3 to level 2 gives red light (656 nm), and from level 4 to level 2 blue-green light (486 nm). This is how Bohr explained hydrogen's line spectrum.
A:adimlar.5.metin: Quantum mechanics was built in the 1920s. Use the switch to go from Bohr's orbit to the modern model.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: In the modern model, which is true about the electron?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: Its position is known only as a probability
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: In quantum mechanics, an electron's position and speed cannot both be known exactly at the same time. So only probability is calculated. In the dark parts of the cloud the chance of finding it is high.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: That was Bohr's idea. In the modern model there is no exact orbit.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The nucleus holds protons and neutrons. Electrons are around the nucleus.
A:kapanis.0: For Dalton (1803-1808), the atom is a solid sphere that cannot be divided.
A:kapanis.1: In 1897 Thomson showed that cathode rays are made of negatively charged electrons. In the plum pudding model he proposed in 1904, the atom is a positive sphere with electrons embedded in it.
A:kapanis.2: Rutherford's gold foil experiment (1909-1911) showed that the atom is mostly empty space. The mass is packed into a small, positively charged nucleus.
A:kapanis.3: For Bohr (1913), electrons move in certain energy levels. An electron that drops to a lower level gives off light of a certain color.
A:kapanis.4: In the modern model the position of the electron cannot be known exactly. Only the probability of finding it, its orbital, is calculated.
